articles.title: Trump ties Camp Lejeune toxic water settlements to GOP midterm results
articles.summary: President Trump told an audience in North Carolina that if Republicans retain control of Congress in the upcoming November midterm elections, he would direct the Justice Department to quickly settle “all remaining legitimate claims” related to contaminated water at the nearby Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, where thousands of cases remain unresolved. “If we don’t…
articles.body:
President Trump told an audience in North Carolina that if Republicans retain control of Congress in the upcoming November midterm elections, he would direct the Justice Department to quickly settle “all remaining legitimate claims” related to contaminated water at the nearby Marine Corps Base Camp Lejeune, where thousands of cases remain unresolved.

“If we don’t win, there’s no money,” Trump said Tuesday night at a campaign rally in Greenville. “If we do win, you’re getting it. It’s going to be finally over with, that nightmare that’s been going on for so many years. We will never abandon the heroes who served America.”

Camp Lejeune is notorious for its toxic water, which service members and their families drank and bathed in from 1953 to 1987. The water supply was contaminated with trichloroethylene (TCE), a colorless solvent that was widely used in industry to clean metal starting in the 1920s. It can remain in groundwater for long periods of time and sicken those who are exposed to it with serious illnesses including cancer and Parkinson’s disease.

Though TCE contaminated the base’s water supply for nearly 30 years, military officials did not discover the water quality was compromised until 1982.

The Promise to Address Comprehensive Toxics Act, passed in 2022, allows individuals to seek benefits from the Department of Veterans Affairs or sue the government for illness caused by the contaminated water.

The base is now at the center of dozens of civil lawsuits against the U.S. government for the hazardous conditions there, with the first trial to start next week.

In lieu of litigation, the Justice Department and the Navy in 2023 offered its Elective Option settlement program to provide faster payouts to people with qualifying illnesses, with the Justice Department in March vowing to speed up settlement offers.

But the program, which includes more than 400,000 unsettled claims, has its own set of issues as several claimants have argued the government denied them compensation or offered less than they should have received.

Conservative activist Laura Loomer, a defender of Trump, on Monday accused Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward, the man overseeing the settlement efforts, of “sending these veterans insulting lowball offers designed to insult and belittle their suffering.”

“This is a political disaster waiting to happen,” she wrote on the social platform X . “Let’s be clear: Democrats are 100% going to weaponize this against President Trump and try to hurt him with veterans heading into the midterms in two weeks.”

On Tuesday Trump claimed that his administration had delivered $1 billion in cash settlements to veterans and families affected by the contamination.

He added that if GOP candidates “win the House and the Senate,” he would direct “the Department of Justice to settle all remaining legitimate claims as soon as possible.”

“We don’t want to give any to the trial lawyers. We’ve given a lot of money to — no trial lawyers, if you don’t mind — we want it to go to the families, not to the lawyers.”

articles.title: China expresses ‘firm opposition’ to Trump administration sanctions tied to former Google engineer
articles.summary: China slammed the Trump administration’s move to sanction five Chinese companies linked to a former Google engineer accused of intellectual property theft, calling it “egregious.” The State Department announced the sanctions on Monday, stating the firms are connected to Chinese national Linwei Ding, who was convicted earlier this year of stealing AI-related trade secrets from…
articles.body:
China slammed the Trump administration’s move to sanction five Chinese companies linked to a former Google engineer accused of intellectual property theft, calling it “egregious.”

The State Department announced the sanctions on Monday, stating the firms are connected to Chinese national Linwei Ding, who was convicted earlier this year of stealing AI-related trade secrets from Google.

The imposition of these sanctions “severely harms the legitimate rights and interests” of Chinese businesses, the country’s Commerce Ministry said in a statement, which was shared by The Associated Press . “The nature of this act is egregious. China firms opposes this.”

The ministry pressed the U.S. to “correct its erroneous practice,” adding Beijing would “take necessary measures,” the news wire added.

Among the sanctioned entities were Shanghai Zhisuan Technology Co., a software platform company founded by Ding, and the China-based venture capital firm MiraclePlus, which the State Department said gave seed capital for Zhisuan. Three other affiliated venture capital firms were also sanctioned.

MiraclePlus released a statement on Tuesday denying it invested in Zhisuan, writing, “We are actively communicating with the relevant parties and hope to lift the sanctions as soon as possible.”

“We believe that there are fair and reasonable processes and systems in place, and that through honest communication, this matter will ultimately be resolved appropriately,” the company added.

Ding was found guilty of seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of thefts of trade secrets, after stealing more than 2,000 pages of confidential information from Google.

“The United States has long been a leader in developing emerging technology. This theft of trade secrets is a serious threat to U.S. economic, foreign policy, and national security interests,” State Department spokesperson Thomas Pigott wrote in a statement Monday.

According to prosecutors, Ding downloaded the tranche of documents, which contained information about Google’s chips and the software used to connect them to a supercomputer, to his personal computer less than two weeks before he resigned. He then told potential investors he could build an AI supercomputer using Google’s technology.

A federal judge in San Francisco later dropped the espionage charges but sentenced Ding to nearly one year in prison, with two years of supervised release.

The Associated Press contributed reporting.

articles.title: Poll: Most Americans confident in safety of routine childhood vaccines
articles.summary: Most adults remain confident in the safety of long-standing childhood vaccines, though people’s views of the COVID-19 vaccine are heavily polarized, according to a new poll from health research organization KFF. More than 80 percent of American respondents said they’re “very” or “somewhat” confident that the polio vaccine and the measles, mumps and rubella…
articles.body:
Most adults remain confident in the safety of long-standing childhood vaccines , though people’s views of the COVID-19 vaccine are heavily polarized, according to a new poll from health research organization KFF.

More than 80 percent of American respondents said they’re “very” or “somewhat” confident that the polio vaccine and the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine are safe for kids. Those views were somewhat partisan, with Republican respondents being 79 percent confident in the polio vaccine and 77 percent in the MMR one, compared with 87 percent for polio and 91 percent for MMR among Democrats.

Even self-described supporters of the “Make America Healthy Again” (MAHA) movement — which has often been associated with vaccine skepticism — said they have confidence in the safety of MMR and polio vaccines.

A smaller majority of Republicans, 56 percent, said they are confident in the safety of the flu shot, compared with 83 percent of Democrats.

But the partisan divide was much more pronounced with the COVID-19 vaccine and the hepatitis B vaccine.

While half of respondents overall said they are confident the COVID-19 vaccines are safe for children, just 21 percent of Republicans expressed those views, compared with 77 percent of Democrats.

Only 28 percent of MAHA supporters said they are confident in the safety of COVID-19 vaccines for children.

When asked about the hepatitis B vaccine, 88 percent of Democrats and 59 percent of Republicans said they thought the shots were safe.

The Trump administration is trying to remove the universal recommendation that all children get vaccinated at birth against hepatitis B, though the effort has been blocked by a federal court .

An executive order signed by President Trump in August called for the reduction in the number of diseases targeted by routine childhood vaccination from 17 to 11, and it called for the MMR vaccines to be administered as separate vaccines, among other directives.

Trump falsely said the combined MMR vaccine is “lethal” and that spacing out and separating doses of childhood vaccines would reduce autism rates.

There is no evidence to support his claims, but the poll found about half of parents incorrectly believe children are healthier when vaccines are spaced out and they do not get multiple shots in one visit.

The survey was conducted online and by phone from Sept. 16-21. Researchers surveyed a nationally representative sample of 1,328 adults; the margin of error was 3 percentage points, and potentially higher for some subgroups.

articles.title: Will TP-Link really make routers in the US? Here’s what it told us
articles.summary: TP-Link has signed a letter of intent to manufacture routers in Mississippi — in an attempt to get the FCC to approve its Wi-Fi 8 routers for import and sale.
articles.body: TP-Link, one of the world’s leading manufacturers of consumer Wi-Fi routers, is in a precarious position in the US. The company just launched its first Wi-Fi 8 routers, but can’t bring them here because of President Donald Trump’s foreign router ban. Even though competitors Netgear and Asus make their routers in Asia, they’ve mysteriously obtained blanket waivers for all their new gear; perhaps because of alleged ties to China, TP-Link hasn’t managed to get such a waiver yet. But TP-Link is willing to do something those companies weren’t — to invest nearly $1 billion to make routers in the United States, creating “hundreds of high-paying research and development, manufacturing, and construction jobs for American workers over the next four years,” according to a letter TP-Link sent to the FCC. This week, it announced a letter of intent with US contract manufacturer Key Tronic to begin “domestic assembly” of its Wi-Fi 8 routers in Corinth, Mississippi. It could begin producing routers “as early as next year.” Intriguingly, this might not just be slapping boards into a plastic box. “If you look at what we do with the products in Vietnam, you’ve got raw components coming in and you’ve got completed, tested, shrink-wrapped products coming out,” TP-Link corporate affairs officer Steve Kovsky tells The Verge. “You’ve got surface-mount technology, many layers of testing quality control, we’re doing plastic injection molding, and as far as I know that is what we intend to do in Mississippi.” But how likely is that “letter of intent” to turn into a true manufacturing plant? After talking to Kovsky, it sounds like the stars might need to align. What is TP-Link waiting for? A deal with the Federal Communications Commission. Kovksy confirms the offer hinges on the FCC granting that router ban waiver — formally known as “conditional approval” — before it can proceed. Kovsky wouldn’t tell me how long ago TP-Link applied for that waiver, but it sounds like the FCC hasn’t yet given the company any idea whether it’ll be approved. TP-Link had to provide lots of info about the company’s structure, ownership, and supply chain, but Kovksy confirms the FCC hasn’t asked any follow-up questions about other topics, and he says the FCC doesn’t exactly tell companies when it denies conditional approval. “We’re looking at offering total transparency to these agencies, and we’re open to negotiations,” he says. “Nothing is written in stone.” Why does TP-Link need an import waiver if it’ll be building routers in the US? “I have asked that question myself,” Kovsky tells The Verge. The short answer is components. Even though TP-Link buys its chipsets from US companies like Qualcomm and Broadcom, those companies don’t actually produce those chips in the US. “Do they count as US product?” Kovsky rhetorically asks. “It’s not a lock, and we would rather have [the waiver],” he says. Why might the FCC hesitate? Five states have now sued over TP-Link’s alleged ties to China, and many more are directly asking the FCC not to grant a waiver, claiming the company dominates the consumer router market, that it’s a Chinese company posing as a US one, that the routers have brought serious security vulnerabilities into US homes, and more. Kovksy suggests it’s all based on misinformation, even the company’s market share: “It’s about 9 to 10 percent, which is like top three. It’s a good number, but we do not have an overwhelming share of the US market.” TP-Link’s website clarifies that it has 10 percent market share when you count all the routers that internet providers put into people’s homes. “We do not sell customer data or share it with any government ever. We never will. We do not allow backdoors in our products. We are not susceptible to malware or vulnerabilities to an extent that’s greater than any other manufacturer in this category to my knowledge,” Kovsky says. It’s certainly true that Netgear routers got a blanket waiver despite being similarly implicated in some security scandals and Chinese hacks. I’ll say it once more: The router ban isn’t about security. If it gets the waiver, does TP-Link intend to produce all US-bound routers in the US? TP-Link is not willing to commit to that yet. “I don’t think that’s entirely determined,” Kovksy says. “Some of that is going to be: What are the FCC and the administration really trying to achieve?” The administration already has a stated goal, though: It wants Made-in-USA products where at least 65 percent of their components are also made here. Kovsky says that TP-Link would be “happy to comply with that, to the extent that it can continue to produce products that meet its criteria for quality and affordability.” “That is going to be challenging, certainly in the short term, [because] those components for the most part just are not produced in the US,” Kovsky says. He says TP-Link believes components will become more available and affordable if the US pushes other manufacturers to invest, but the waiver isn’t the only factor in its decision. If it gets the waiver, will TP-Link invest, or will it need to find an inexpensive source of components or other things before it can go ahead? “I think those are probably going to be business decisions that the CEO will ultimately have to make,” Kovksy begins. “Well, I hope he doesn’t have to make those decisions, frankly, that everything falls in line. He is very committed to making this investment,” he says. Notably, TP-Link would not confirm Kovsky’s suggestion that it might completely manufacture routers in the US and only source the raw components. I told the company that if I could say TP-Link was committed to anything other than “final assembly,” it’d be well worth sharing with readers. “At this stage, TP-Link is not sharing specific job numbers or detailed technical details of the assembly process beyond what’s in today’s press release,” third-party spokesperson Ricca Silverio told me. I don’t think this is Foxconn in Wisconsin all over again because TP-Link probably won’t get its conditional approval, let alone invest in empty buildings. Foreign gadget bans from President Trump and FCC Chairman Brendan Carr seem explicitly designed to target companies China hawks claim to be worried about, like DJI or Unitree, while letting favored companies through. But the hawks, including a coalition of congresspeople led by Sen. Tom Cotton (R-AR), seem to hate TP-Link, too.

articles.title: Judge orders Meta to pay New Mexico $25B in Cambridge Analytica case
articles.summary: A judge in New Mexico ordered the technology giant Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for misleading users about its privacy and content policies. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez (D) announced the judge’s order Wednesday, calling it “one of the single largest — if not the largest —…
articles.body:
A judge in New Mexico ordered the technology giant Meta to pay $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for misleading users about its privacy and content policies.

New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez (D) announced the judge’s order Wednesday, calling it “one of the single largest — if not the largest — single state verdict against the company in American history.”

“Today’s judgement from a state, which admittedly is not very big in terms of population, should be a clear warning to everyone in Big Tech, Mr. [Mark] Zuckerberg, Meta, social media companies, indeed AI companies,” Torrez said at a press conference.

The order from Santa Fe Judge Francis Mathew comes just weeks after jurors found Meta liable for more than 43 million violations of New Mexico’s consumer protection laws when the British consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested data from Facebook users for political ads during the 2016 election.

Following an expected appeals process, Torrez said the payment from Meta will be put toward public education in the state.

New Mexico was one of just two states that chose not to join the 48-state settlement with Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram. The company agreed to pay $459 million as part of that settlement.

Attorneys for New Mexico originally sought $35 billion to $40 billion, suggesting the order would need to impact Meta’s stock price to establish real change, The Associated Press reported. Meta’s lawyers argued to pay no more than $3.4 billion, claiming anything more than $34 billion would violate due process.

Torrez told reporters he expects Meta to appeal, but New Mexico intends “to do everything in our power to make sure that those resources are eventually delivered” to the state.

“The fact that we received a judgment today that is less than the total statutory max shouldn’t be mistaken for the larger message,” Torrez said, adding the previously settled states “are sharing $459 million for the conduct at issue, and New Mexico just received a $25 billion judgement.”

“So I’ll leave it to you to determine whether and to what extent that counts as a victory,” he told reporters.

Wednesday’s order is the latest in a string of legal battles over the Cambridge Analytica scandal. The Supreme Court in 2024 heard Facebook’s bid to block a shareholder lawsuit over the Cambridge Analytica data scandal from moving forward.

Shareholders sued the social media company after the public became widely aware of the scandal in 2018, accusing Facebook of misleading investors in an earlier securities filing by failing to mention Cambridge Analytica’s misuse of user data.

While the tech giant acknowledged in a 2016 filing that improper third-party use of its data could harm its business, it did not mention Cambridge Analytica. As a result, the shareholders argue, they were led to believe that no such incident had occurred.

Facebook argued its statements in the risk disclosure section of the securities filing were only about future events and did not suggest that such an event had never taken place.

The Supreme Court later dismissed the case without issuing a ruling on the merits.

articles.title: UN climate report says world will fail 1.5-degree Paris goal but argues for keeping overshoot brief
articles.summary: A new United Nations climate report released Wednesday said that while global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5-degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, urgent and steep cuts to emissions can help reduce the overshoot. The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return published by the U.N. Environment Programme, looks at the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario, in…
articles.body:
A new United Nations climate report released Wednesday said that while global temperatures are set to exceed 1.5-degree Celsius above pre-industrial levels, urgent and steep cuts to emissions can help reduce the overshoot.

The Emissions Gap Report 2026: The Point of Return published by the U.N. Environment Programme , looks at the “lowest possible” overshoot scenario, in which peak warming can be limited to 1.7-1.8 degrees Celsius in the middle of the century, according to a press release from the U.N.

“The chance to keep global warming below 1.5°C with no overshoot is gone,” the UNEP wrote in a post on social platform X. “But urgent action can still limit the overshoot and bring warming back to 1.5°C by 2100.”

To achieve the target of limiting overshoot and returning to the 1.5-degree Celsius target laid out in the 2015 Paris Climate Agreement, global greenhouse gas emissions would have to be reduced by 18 percent by 2030, 45 percent by 2035 and 69 percent by 2040, relative to 2025 levels, according to a press release from UNEP .

“By contrast, the full implementation of Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs) would only reduce emissions by 5-8 per cent by 2030 and 11-15 per cent by 2035, relative to 2025 levels,” the release said.

The report found that if countries follow their current policies, warming levels could reach 2.8 degrees Celsius within the century and increase after. If all existing emissions reduction pledges are fulfilled, warming would be limited to 2.6 degrees Celsius, projections that the UNEP said are “are worse than last year’s projections due to the withdrawal of the United States of America from the Paris Agreement and revised estimates of historical emissions.”

Earlier this year in January , President Trump’s move to pull the U.S. from the Paris Climate Agreement took effect. The president signed an executive order to withdraw U.S. from the agreement soon after he took office last year. Trump, in his first term, also withdrew the U.S. from the agreement before former President Biden rejoined the pact.

In the U.N. release, UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen warned that every additional fraction of a degree and additional year of warming above 1.5 degrees Celsius increases the chance of climate impacts and risks.

She pointed to “the deadly floods, heatwaves and wildfires that have plagued many nations this year.”

“So, we must pull out all the stops to minimize peak warming and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century”, she said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio says he’s not worried about the safety of NFL players, coaches and fans in France, where the league will play a game on Sunday amid widespread rioting across the country.

“I was never planning to go anyways,” he added of the game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and New Orleans Saints, slated for 9 a.m. EDT at Stade de France near Paris.

France has been hit by widespread political protests in recent days, some of which have devolved into violent rioting and looting in major cities.

Many on the political right in the U.S. have blamed the social unrest in France on immigration and pointed to it as a result of progressive ideology run amok.

The NFL, meanwhile, is playing a record 11 games overseas this season as the most popular U.S. sports league works to grow its brand internationally.

The league has already staged games in London, Australia and Brazil, with more slated before the regular season concludes in December.

articles.title: NSA warns organizations to patch security flaws identified by AI
articles.summary: The National Security Agency (NSA) warned organizations Wednesday to immediately patch a pair of security flaws or take their systems offline after artificial intelligence discovered vulnerabilities in a key programming language. “Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities,” the NSA’s cyber…
articles.body:
The National Security Agency (NSA) warned organizations Wednesday to immediately patch a pair of security flaws or take their systems offline after artificial intelligence discovered vulnerabilities in a key programming language.

“Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities,” the NSA’s cyber division wrote in a post on the social platform X.

“These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database,” the agency continued. “If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.”

PHP is a programming language frequently used in web development and is often referred to as the “backbone of the web.” It powers 70 percent of all websites around the world, including popular platforms like WordPress and Wikipedia’s MediaWiki.

The cyber division of the FBI similarly urged organizations to act quickly and users to monitor web services for suspicious activity. Users were told to report “signs of compromise” to a local FBI field office or the Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Developers of the PHP language released fixes to the vulnerabilities Wednesday morning after government websites in Europe and elsewhere went dark, urging users to “update immediately.”

The bug identified by security researchers has been present in the code for 14 years, OpenAI President Greg Brockman said Wednesday.

A limited version of the bug was initially discovered in 2024 but wasn’t deemed significant, he noted. In August, security researchers working with an OpenAI initiative and using the company’s GPT-5.6 Sol model found a version of the vulnerability.

“Over the past two months, we have been leading a coalition to mitigate one of the most severe bugs in open source software found in recent memory,” Brockman wrote on X.

“This vulnerability allows any attacker to execute code on nearly all deployed PHP application, effectively allowing them to exfiltrate private user data or modifying the site however they want,” he added.

OpenAI also released a PHP version checker within its Codex system to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions.

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in malware history,” researchers at Wiz wrote in a blog post Wednesday.

AI developers have often touted the technology’s ability to spot security vulnerabilities at significantly faster rates than humans or traditional computer systems, while warning the same tools can also be employed by bad actors.

articles.title: Meta ordered to pay $25 billion in penalties over the Cambridge Analytica scandal
articles.summary: A New Mexico court ordered Meta to pay $25 billion for misleading the public about its privacy and misinformation measures stemming from the Cambridge Analytica scandal.
articles.body: The Cambridge Analytica scandal has come back to haunt Meta after a New Mexico judge ordered it to pay $25 billion in penalties for more than 43 million violations of the state’s unfair practices law. The ruling marks the biggest legal hit Meta has taken this year, even as it’s faced several other losses or settlements. A New Mexico jury ruled in September that Meta misled consumers over how it protected their data and prevented misinformation and hate speech on its platforms. The case stemmed from a 2021 complaint in the wake of the revelations a few years earlier that UK political consultancy Cambridge Analytica harvested data from millions of Facebook accounts to pinpoint messages that would resonate with voters leading up to President Donald Trump’s first election. The judge found that the “extraordinary number of willful violations found by the jury, the duration and repetition of the conduct, the breadth of subjects on which violations occurred, the involvement of senior Facebook leadership,” and other factors justified the highest penalty allowed under the law, at $5,000 per violation. That brings the total civil penalties to more than $219 billion, but the judge reduced it to $25 billion. “This ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to this enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” Meta’s chief legal officer C.J. Mahoney said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.” Even this smaller sum is “one of the largest financial penalties against a corporation in U.S. history,” according to the AG’s office, and dwarfs other recent rulings and settlements involving Meta. In another landmark ruling in New Mexico state court, Meta was ordered to pay a total of nearly $1 billion in civil penalties and abatement for misleading the public about the safety of its products. In a separate agreement with most other state AGs, Meta settled an array of kids online safety complaints for $17.1 billion — but $5.3 billion of that is contingent on YouTube and TikTok installing similar measures. New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez issued a triumphant statement after the latest in his string of wins against Meta (though the company managed to fight off many of the business changes the AG asked for in the remedies portion of the kids online safety case). “This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,” Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law.” Update, October 21st: Added statement from Meta.

articles.title: The internet is having a very bad cybersecurity day | TechCrunch
articles.summary: From AI-discovered PHP vulnerabilities to flaws in Node.js and popular AI tool LiteLLM, cybersecurity teams have plenty to worry about this week.
articles.body:
The internet is having a bad day, from a cybersecurity perspective. Government websites around the world went offline , Reuters reported, after AI discovered critical security vulnerabilities that impacted the programming language PHP . The issues were severe enough that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) advised organizations using PHP on their systems to either immediately update or take their systems offline until they could.

But the PHP update wasn’t the only headache cybersecurity folks were facing on Wednesday. Node.js , the open-source JavaScript runtime environment, also dropped a security surprise of its own when it shared that four high-severity vulnerabilities were just patched in its latest release. One allowed remote code execution, and two others would have permitted a TLS validation bypass, potentially allowing attackers to bypass checks intended to verify a server’s identity.

In addition, LiteLLM, a popular open source proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, was compromised by an attacker who injected malicious code, the company shared in a post on X on Wednesday afternoon. The malicious artifacts were published to PyPI (Python Package Index), Docker Hub , and GHCR (GitHub Container Registry), the post noted.

The malicious code was said to include an information stealer that targeted cloud credentials, passwords, and AI service credentials, in addition to a remote access trojan that could allow hackers to execute commands on compromised systems.

LiteLLM said it has now removed the malicious releases and images and advised anyone who installed them to follow the remediation guidance it provided.

And wait, there’s more! An Indian certificate authority, eMudhra, had its private keys compromised , potentially allowing attackers to issue fraudulent certificates and impersonate legitimate websites. Security pros have called this a massive cleanup job and one that’s “bigger than Heartbleed .” (The latter is a reference to the critical security vulnerability in the OpenSSL cryptographic software library).

These issues come on the heels of other security breaches and hacks, including the breach of the cloud-native database-as-a-service, TiDB Cloud, which the company announced on Monday. Other hackers have been exploiting four patched Plex Media Server flaws, collectively called Plex2Shell. And last week, cybersecurity company BeyondTrust warned customers to patch a critical zero-day in its Remote Support product, which had been exploited since August.

Though the issues were unrelated to each other, their back-to-back arrival highlights the challenges cybersecurity teams now face. This is particularly important as AI could make it easier for attackers to exploit vulnerabilities once discovered.

articles.title: GM is betting compute and AI will help it compete with Chinese automakers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: To compete with Tesla, Rivian, and a host of Chinese automakers, GM’s fourth-gen EV platform will roll out a new central computer and electrical architecture that will debut in 2028 in the Cadillac Escalade IQ.
articles.body:
When GM announced its new fourth-generation EV platform on Wednesday, what the automaker didn’t share was almost as notable as what it did.

The new EV platform, part of a series of technology-focused announced during its annual GM Forward event in New York, didn’t talk about suspension geometries, dash-to-axle ratios, and torsional rigidity, all nerdy automotive terms that translate to how people will experience a car. Is it supple or sporty? Does it have a refined stance? When it hits a pothole, does it feel like a bank vault or a paper plate?

Instead, GM’s announcement centered on novel battery chemistries, revamped electric motors, and an entirely new central computing platform and electrical architecture that will connect every system in the car, including acceleration and power, steering, braking, and active safety features as well as software. Lots and lots of software.

“We think vehicles can become a more capable and helpful part of everyday life if we make them spaces that understand context, reduce friction, and give people back moments that would otherwise be consumed by the demands of the road,” Sterling Anderson, executive vice president, global product, and chief product officer at GM, told TechCrunch in a recent interview.

That sure doesn’t sound like a traditional automaker’s pitch. Then again, since the arrival of Tesla, Rivian, and Chinese automakers, the industry hasn’t been the same. Ride and handling still matter, but they’re table stakes. What sets vehicles apart today is largely defined by software.

Anderson has talked about this future GM before. Last year, the company announced plans to overhaul the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant.

This year, GM is providing more details and dates. This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also rollout an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over.

European and U.S. automakers have spent years chasing the prospect of software-defined vehicles, but have often fallen short. Volkswagen Group had so much trouble with its own in-house effort, including its troubled Cariad unit, that it struck a $5.8 billion joint venture deal with relative newcomer Rivian.

GM has been on its own capitally intensive software adventure. The company has bet heavily on software in recent years. It ditched the popular smartphone projection technology Apple CarPlay for nearly all of its EVs, and instead turned to a Google-based infotainment system, which is actually quite capable even if it doesn’t yet live up to the standards set by Tesla and Rivian.

It’s poured billions into software and autonomous vehicle technology development too. GM’s capitalized software amortization expense in 2025 was $866 million, which gives a sense of how much it is spending even as it spreads out the cost over years.

Like many legacy automakers, GM has come to the conclusion that the old approach to electronics, which scattered computer chips throughout the vehicle, was holding it back.

For fourth-generation EVs, GM will centralize much of those functions on a Central Compute Unit (CCU) that’s 40-times more powerful than its existing systems. Eliminating smaller chips on the edges will help trim wiring by 30%, saving weight and simplifying assembly.

GM notes that this new CCU will work on fossil fuel models, too, though it will debut in the Cadillac Escalade IQ, a vehicle that is shaping up to be the automaker’s technological flagship.

The CCU will handle the usual propulsion and chassis controls, but also perception and active safety. That should help pave the way for more advanced autonomy features, which GM also announced on Wednesday.

Such a move was perhaps inevitable. Pressure on automakers has been building on all sides.

Domestically, Tesla has been pushing the boundaries of autonomy, in part because it developed a true software-defined vehicle.

Automakers like GM are also feeling pressure from Chinese manufacturers, which have shortened development cycles to two to three years, down from the usual four to five years.

GM intends to match that cadence. Alongside announcements about battery chemistries and autonomy, GM outlined how enterprise AI tools have sped up vehicle development across every sector as it pushes to slash its traditional four-to-five-year development timeline in half.

GM gave a brief glimpse of its revamped development strategy. One example: engineers went through 300,000 virtual designs of a new lithium-manganese-rich battery pack before they assembled the first physical prototype. That helped the concept move to an approved program in one month.

Such speed will help GM save costs as it races to preserve profitability amid a historic upheaval in the automotive industry. But will it be enough to catapult it back into the leadership position it once enjoyed?

The rise of Chinese automakers won’t make it easy. Their factories are capable of producing far more than Chinese consumers can absorb, and coupled with government subsidies and cheaper labor, these vehicles have flooded markets from Europe to South America with inexpensive vehicles.

Chinese automaker’s cost advantage is so steep that, without trade barriers, “they will pretty much demolish most other companies in the world,” Elon Musk said in a 2024 earnings call. In response, he has been trying to pivot Tesla from an automotive company to an AI and robotics company.

GM’s move into autonomy signals a similar shift. But to deliver true autonomy, GM realized it didn’t have the platform it needed. With a new architecture, it should have a fighting chance.

articles.title: PHP: The three letters that shut down sites all over the internet today
articles.summary: Patches have been released to fix the AI-discovered “PHP2Shell” issue, but with millions of servers potentially vulnerable, the race is on to apply the updates and secure data.
articles.body: Two bugs found with AI are behind major issues today for 4chan, DeviantArt, Wikipedia, and the blog where the bar around the corner posts pictures of people’s dogs. The “critical vulnerabilities” were discovered in the PHP programming language, which underpins much of the internet, including any site built on WordPress. But it’s far bigger than that. Some Dutch and Finnish government agencies took their sites down as a precaution. The NSA Cybersecurity account on X recommended that organizations take their systems offline if “an immediate update is not feasible,” as did the UK’s National Cyber Security Center. Even Pokémon Home and Pokémon Champions were taken offline, Kotaku reports. The vulnerability isn’t exactly new. It’s been present in PHP for roughly 20 years, but exploiting it “required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve,” according to security firm Wiz. However, powerful AI models have made it much easier to turn that kind of obscure bug into dangerous vulnerabilities. As a casual internet user, you might be wondering what exactly the barrage of jargon like “RCE via OOM corruption” means, how concerned you should be, and how exactly a vulnerability this severe flew under the radar for so long. What is PHP? W3Techs, a survey service, says that the PHP programming language is used by “69.3 percent of all the websites whose server-side programming language we know,” including popular sites like Wikipedia and WordPress. The internet security site VirusTotal says its scanner currently registers about 3.8 million sites running PHP with at least one port open. What happened? According to OpenAI, an AI security group called Calif identified a “critical” PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz independently discovered and reported the vulnerabilities using AI. The PHP Foundation says that an exploit for one of the vulnerabilities “was theorized” in 2024, but “no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.” Now the PHP Group says hackers could use the two vulnerabilities for “unauthenticated remote code execution,” like running their own code, changing content, and accessing a site’s stored data without needing an administrator login or password. > RCE via OOM corruption, CVE-2026-109618 (GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w): out-of-memory handling can interrupt PHP while internal request data is only partially initialized. Request cleanup may then treat the invalid data as valid. > RCE via stale global state, CVE-2026-109619 (GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp): request-owned internal state can survive after its backing memory has been freed. A later request handled by the same worker may use that stale state before normal initialization resets it. How serious is it? Very. The PHP Group says that basically any site running PHP is at risk. OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research, said: “We consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.” And Wiz said it’s “among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered … in software history.” Last night, the CTO of Cloudflare said that it was “seeing early attacks emerging.” It’s hard to understate just how bad this could get. The vulnerabilities could allow an attacker to take full control of a server. That includes gaining access to passwords, API keys, cryptographic certificates, and databases of sensitive information. They could also execute code on those servers, turning them into vectors to attack other vulnerable servers. And, thanks to AI, it’s relatively trivial for a determined hacker to exploit these flaws now that they have been revealed. What can I do? As a user, not much. The vulnerability affects servers running PHP and doesn’t necessarily target users directly, but it could use compromised sites to spread malware and steal other valuable data. If you’re feeling extra cautious, check the social accounts of sites and services you frequently use to see if they’ve posted any updates before visiting. If you have a website, even a simple blog, it’s time to check what version of PHP your site uses, if any. If you’re using a service like Squarespace or Wix, you’re in the clear, as those don’t support PHP. Customers of Hostinger, GoDaddy, Bluehost, or other web hosting services should be more cautious. GoDaddy says that any site using PHP should assume it is affected and update to the fixed release as soon as possible. It also says that sites running PHP 8.1 or older should upgrade to a newer version, as they’re no longer supported and there will not be an official fix coming. Those on a managed hosting service should check with their provider to see when they should expect the fix to be deployed. If you sell products or services or have any sensitive data on your servers at all, it’s best to disable your site until your host patches their version of PHP.

articles.title: Major hostilities brewing? US orders departure of some embassy staff, families from Gulf region
articles.summary: Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & NatSec newsletter {beacon} Defense &National Security Defense &National Security The Big Story Major hostilities brewing? US orders departure of some embassy staff, families from Gulf region The State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as the…
articles.body:
Major hostilities brewing? US orders departure of some embassy staff, families from Gulf region

The State Department ordered the departure of nonemergency U.S. government employees and their family members from Saudi Arabia on Wednesday as the Iranian-backed Houthis have continued to attack the country.

“As the Department has repeatedly emphasized, the hostilities have the potential to escalate rapidly , including beyond that immediate area,” a State Department spokesperson told The Hill.

“The safety and security of Department personnel and their families remain our highest priority , and we will continue to take all necessary steps to protect and support them as they return to the U.S.,” the spokesperson said in a statement.

Reuters reported Wednesday that the U.S. government is preparing to issue an ordered departure of some personnel and family members from U.S. embassies across the Gulf .

And The Agence France-Presse later reported that the U.S. ordered families of embassy staff in the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain to leave, citing a diplomatic source.

Asked about the reports, Trump feigned ignorance, telling journalist: “I don’t know that they are. You are telling me something — I wouldn’t know that .”

The new order comes as the Houthis are engaged in a war against the Saudi-backed Yemeni government and have been attacking infrastructure inside Saudi Arabia , including civilian airports and other critical sites that have led to civilian casualties.

Saudi Arabia’s air defense intercepted a drone targeting Aramco’s Shaybah oilfield on Wednesday, but two people were killed and another two were injured from the falling debris, the nation’s energy ministry said.

Welcome to The Hill’s Defense & National Security newsletter, I’m Ellen Mitchell — your guide to the latest developments at the Pentagon, on Capitol Hill and beyond.

articles.title: PHP2Shell: Governments on high alert over critical website flaw; Wikipedia, hospitals, school portals go dark; what users should know
articles.summary: A large chunk of the internet went offline on Wednesday, and most of it was switched off on purpose.
articles.body: A large chunk of the internet went offline on Wednesday, and most of it was switched off on purpose. Government websites in the Netherlands, Finland, France and Denmark, along with universities, hospitals and sites as big as Wikipedia, pulled systems down after two serious security flaws were found in PHP. Most people have never heard of PHP, but it is the software running behind roughly 70% of all websites, from news sites and online shops to personal blogs.The flaws, now nicknamed PHP2Shell, let a hacker take over the computer that runs a website without needing a password. They had been hiding in PHP's code for more than a decade, and it took artificial intelligence (AI) to find them. PHP's developers released a fix on October 21, but hackers moved within hours to attack websites that hadn't updated yet. Cyber security agencies in the US and the UK have told website owners to install the fix right away or take their sites offline until they can.The list of affected sites shows how far PHP reaches. The Dutch government's own cyber security agency shut its website as a precaution. Finland took several government online services offline, France's Interior Ministry put all its websites into maintenance mode, and Denmark shut its national school communication platform. In the Netherlands, the Port of Rotterdam, the national football association, several hospitals and the five largest political parties also took their sites down. The Internet Archive went offline briefly, and online forums 4chan and DeviantArt ran into trouble. Even Pokémon Home and Pokémon Champions were taken offline.Some world leaders got involved too. Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi posted on X: "We have an urgent request for everyone to take action tonight."The rush makes sense once you see how fast hackers moved. Cloudflare, a company that sits in front of millions of websites to protect them, saw thousands of hacking attempts even before the flaws were made public. CEO Matthew Prince said in a post on X that this climbed to tens of thousands within 45 minutes of the announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions by the next morning.PHP is the hidden software behind most websites on the internetThink of a website as having two sides. The side you see is the page in your browser. The side you don't see is a computer, called a server, that builds that page every time you open it. It fetches the right text, images, prices or comments from a database and sends the finished page to your screen. PHP is the language that does this job for a huge share of the web.It has been around since the early 1990s, and it powers WordPress, the tool behind millions of blogs and business websites. It also runs Wikipedia, many government portals, and platforms like Drupal and Joomla that big organisations use to manage their websites. Web tracking firm W3Techs estimates PHP is used by about 69.3% of all websites whose underlying software it can identify.That is why a single flaw in PHP turned into a global problem. Tiffany Farriss, who heads the Drupal Association, told Reuters that any server running a version of PHP from the last 20 years would be vulnerable. "This issue impacts the majority of the internet," she said.PHP is also free and open source, which means anyone can use it. It is looked after by a small non-profit, the PHP Foundation, which has just 13 full-time and part-time engineers maintaining software that much of the internet depends on.The PHP2Shell flaw lets hackers take over a website without a passwordNormally, to change a website or access its stored data, you need an administrator login. PHP2Shell skips that step entirely.The two flaws, officially tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, are both rated 9.2 out of 10 for severity. In simple terms, a hacker can send a website a carefully crafted request that makes PHP run out of memory and stop halfway through its work. That leaves behind some leftover data in the server. The hacker then sends a second request that makes PHP use that leftover data as if it were normal, and that opens the door to running their own commands on the server.Once inside, a hacker can change what a website shows, plant malicious software that infects visitors, or steal what the server stores. That can include usernames and passwords, digital keys that connect the site to other services, and databases with personal information. A second route even lets hackers peek into the server's short-term memory, where they could catch passwords and login details of other people using the site at the same time.Wiz, one of the firms that found the flaws, showed working attacks on fresh WordPress, Drupal and Joomla websites. It also pointed out that the problem is in PHP itself, so even a basic website with nothing complicated on it can be at risk. Every version of PHP going back more than a decade is affected.AI found a flaw that had been hiding for over a decadeThe bugs were found by two security firms working separately. Calif says it spotted them on August 1 with the help of an AI model, which OpenAI says was its GPT-5.6 Sol. Wiz found them on August 19 using its own AI tool along with Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.What stands out is that the flaws were not new. PHP's own developers had considered a possible attack along these lines in 2024, but nobody could work out how to make it happen. According to Wiz, turning these bugs into a real attack required so many complex steps that it was at the edge of what human experts could manage. With AI, a single researcher did in a week what would earlier have taken a top team months.The plan was to keep the flaws secret until October 22, giving website companies time to prepare fixes quietly. That plan fell apart when details leaked on online forums and social media on Tuesday. PHP rushed its fix out nearly a day early. Amazon later said its systems saw a hacking attempt on October 17, four days before the public announcement, and nobody yet knows how that attacker found out.OpenAI said in a blog post that the episode shows how AI can uncover security flaws, but also how it can help attackers "rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits." The same kind of AI that found the bug can help hackers study the fix and build an attack in very little time. That is why the window between a fix coming out and attacks starting has shrunk from days to minutes.Most users on the internet can relax, but website owners need to update right awayIf you only browse the web, there isn't much you need to do. The flaw targets the servers that run websites, not your phone or laptop. Still, a hacked website can be used to spread malware or steal data, so stay alert for a few weeks. If a service you use asks you to change your password, do it through the official app or website. Be careful with emails or messages about the PHP flaw that ask you to click links or share details, as scammers often use big news like this as bait.If you run a website, even a small blog, check whether it uses PHP. Sites built on Squarespace or Wix are safe, as those platforms don't use PHP. Automattic, the company behind WordPress.com, says websites it hosts directly, along with Tumblr, are safe. If you installed WordPress yourself or use a hosting company like GoDaddy, Bluehost or Hostinger, contact your provider to find out when the fix will reach your site.The fixed versions of PHP are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35. Websites running PHP 8.1 or older won't get a fix at all, because those versions are no longer supported, so they need to move to a newer version. If your site stores customer details or takes payments and you can't confirm it has been fixed, taking it offline for a few hours is the safer choice. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre has also asked organisations that couldn't update quickly to check whether hackers have already left a hidden way back into their systems.Small websites run by individuals and small businesses are the most at risk, since they often lack a technical team and depend on their hosting company to apply fixes.Sigi Goode, a professor of information systems at the Australian National University, told The Guardian where the real danger lies. "The bigger concern is the websites that are not down today," he said. The websites that went dark on Wednesday were the ones taking the threat seriously. The ones still online without the fix are what hackers will be hunting for in the weeks ahead.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb
articles.summary: It has been a dramatic, public and global response, but the cyber event hasn't happened yet.
articles.body:
I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built.

We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction.

In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building.

The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet.

There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025.

But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution.

Less than two months ago , 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI.

It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant.

The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit.

One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult.

However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI.

The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix.

It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked.

From that point the clock started ticking.

As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site.

"There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University.

"How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers?

"Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out."

But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made.

We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either.

As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success.

Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story.

"We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4.

"We have enormous capability to handle these risks."

But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in.

Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first.

For many it may be a significant repair job, so if there's a web developer in your life you may want to send them thoughts, prayers and maybe a strong coffee.

articles.title: Eiliko maker says it’s hiring an ‘independent security firm’ after Verge report on its insecure robots
articles.summary: ‘We know that words alone will not earn that trust back.’
articles.body: Eiliko, a cute robot charm you can hang on your bag with built-in AI conversations, turned out to be a security nightmare. It told owners that “your secrets are safe with me,” but hackers could easily read complete transcripts of everything we told the toy, and that was just the beginning. The Verge and security researcher Sammy Azdoufal spent over a month trying to get in contact with the company, including emails to Energize Lab CEO and founder Shaw Yeung. Nobody would answer our questions. Now, the company is finally breaking its silence, though its response leaves something to be desired. [Media: “We have confirmed the core issues identified in your reporting and are addressing each of them,” Energize Lab told The Verge in an unsigned statement from a generic email address. The company says it will hire an independent security firm to fully review all of its systems, and has set up a dedicated security@energizelab.com contact email. The company also claims that as of Wednesday, it has “closed all external access to our backend systems” and “disabled the interface that allowed a robot’s responses to be modified remotely.” Energize Labs is also pledging to “no longer store conversation records or the user profiles generated from them,” and says it will delete the conversation records, user profiles, and “avatar images” it has already stored. Notably, the company isn’t promising to get rid of data collection for good. “The long-term memory and custom avatar features will not return until that review confirms they are secure,” it writes, suggesting that Energize Lab does plan to store some personal information once its systems are hardened. Even more notably, Energize Labs’ systems are not yet secure. With Azdoufal’s help, I can confirm that as of the company’s email, it was still storing audio recordings and photos of its customers at unsecured public web addresses with no protection whatsoever. If I gave you a link (which I won’t) you could click and immediately be looking at an owner’s face. Azdoufal also tells me he still has full SSH access to these robots, and that he can still theoretically read transcripts and modify the toy’s behavior. So when Energize Lab says it has “closed all external access,” that doesn’t seem to be accurate. “We know that words alone will not earn that trust back,” Energize Lab tells The Verge. “We intend to earn it through what we do in the coming weeks, and we will keep you informed as we go.” That sounds like a good plan, because some of today’s words still don’t ring true. Here is Energize Lab’s full unsigned statement to The Verge: > Dear Sean, > We sincerely apologize to you and to Mr. Azdoufal for not responding over the past month. This was our failure: After receiving the relevant information, we failed to sync with the technical team in a timely manner, and the subsequent troubleshooting also took some time. We have now set up a dedicated security inbox, security@energizelab.com, which is staffed and monitored. > We thank you and Mr. Azdoufal for bringing these issues to our attention. We have confirmed the core issues identified in your reporting and are addressing each of them. > As of today, we have: > Closed all external access to our backend systems and rotated all access credentials; > Disabled the interface that allowed a robot’s responses to be modified remotely; > Taken the long-term memory feature offline. We no longer store conversation records or the user profiles generated from them; > Taken the custom avatar feature offline. The app now offers built-in avatars only. > We will delete stored conversation records, user profiles, avatar images, and related content. > We are engaging an independent security firm to conduct a full review of our systems. The long-term memory and custom avatar features will not return until that review confirms they are secure. We will share an update on our progress once the review is completed. > We started Energize Lab because we wanted to build small robots that bring a little joy into people’s lives. That idea only works if people can trust what is inside them, and we let them down. We know that words alone will not earn that trust back. We intend to earn it through what we do in the coming weeks, and we will keep you informed as we go. > Sincerely, > Energize Lab Team

articles.title: Americans could be detained for years in popular travel destination, officials warn
articles.summary: Americans are being warned by the State Department that they could face wrongful detention and exit bans in China, with some travelers trapped for years without recourse.
articles.body: Americans traveling to China are being warned about the possibility of detention, electronic surveillance and restrictions that could keep them from returning home, with a travel expert sharing critical information for people to know before they go. The U.S. State Department issued an updated Level 2 "Exercise Increased Caution" advisory for mainland China this week, citing concerns about wrongful detention and restrictions on leaving the country. Travelers are told to be aware that routine professional, academic and personal activities, which carry no risk in Western countries, could be treated as criminal offenses under China's broad security laws. STATE DEPARTMENT ISSUES TRAVEL ADVISORY AS ARRESTS AND EXIT BANS HIT POPULAR DESTINATION The advisory also raises concerns about private communications, warning Americans that emails, texts and social media activity could be monitored by Chinese authorities. "Assume that China's security services can read your emails, texts and social media posts if you send them to or from China," the Oct. 19 advisory states. The State Department said some people have been detained or deported over private messages considered critical of Chinese authorities, even when those messages were sent outside China. The risks extend beyond electronic communications. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The State Department elaborated on possible detention without justification. "The U.S. Department of State has determined that Americans are at serious risk of wrongful detention by the Government of China," the advisory states. Those detained could spend years behind bars with limited contact with family members or U.S. officials, according to the department. Travelers could also face restrictions that prevent them from leaving the country, even if they have not been detained. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE STORIES Chinese authorities have used the "exit bans" during investigations and business or civil disputes. Exit bans have also affected relatives of people under investigation, including children, according to the advisory. Some travelers may not know they're prohibited from leaving until they try to fly home. "Then you realize you're actually not allowed to fly home." "U.S. citizens might only become aware of an exit ban when they attempt to depart China," the State Department said. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Some bans have lasted for years. Officials warn there may be no clear way to challenge them in court. Americans who plan to visit China are advised to travel with a U.S. passport and valid Chinese visa, enroll in the Smart Traveler Enrollment Program and arrange regular check-ins with family members or an employer. Fox News Digital reached out to the U.S. State Department for further comment. "Be aware of your surroundings. Think before you take a picture," advised Bobby Laurie, a longtime travel expert and former flight attendant. "This is one of those situations where maybe you were spotted taking pictures of law enforcement on the street, or you were somewhere you shouldn't have been. Maybe you were inadvertently near a protest on the streets," he added. "Then as your trip comes to an end, you head to the airport. You scan your boarding pass, ready to get through immigration to fly home. And then you realize you're actually not allowed to fly home. There has been an exit ban placed on you." articles.title: Iran: 7 ships hit in the Strait of Hormuz
articles.summary: Iran said Thursday its navy hit seven oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, threatening to exacerbate regional tensions and the global energy crisis that is driving inflation. The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) navy claimed in a statement to have hit four tankers that were transferring oil. The other three ships hit naval…
articles.body:
Iran said Thursday its navy hit seven oil tankers traveling through the Strait of Hormuz, threatening to exacerbate regional tensions and the global energy crisis that is driving inflation.

The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps’s (IRGC) navy claimed in a statement to have hit four tankers that were transferring oil. The other three ships hit naval mines and were immobilized as a result, according to The Associated Press . The IRGC added in its statement that some of the vessels remained ablaze as of Thursday morning.

Iranian state TV also reported that seven ships were hit while traversing the strait. If confirmed, it would mark the largest single-day incident involving vessels in the waterway since the start of the war in February.

The IRGC also issued a warning to the U.S. military against continued efforts to traffic oil tankers through the strait, saying it could cause a response at American bases in the region, per the AP.

The attacks come as the United States and Israel are reportedly drawing up plans for a potential resumption of strikes on Iran after the midterms.

The U.S. also withdrew staff from its embassy in Saudi Arabia this week, as Houthi rebels in Yemen have opened a major new front in the regional conflict.

Iran’s escalation in the Strait of Hormuz highlights that the war is far from over almost eight months after it started, with Tehran flexing its leverage over the crucial shipping corridor.

The attacks come as the international Brent crude oil benchmark was at more than $111 a barrel as of Thursday morning . The national average price for a gallon of gas was $4.27.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this week that lower oil prices were dependent “on what happens with the Iran conflict,” and he said the U.S. is being hit with an “energy shock” but argued “core inflation is down.”

While the U.S.-Iran war has cooled down since intense fighting in the spring, tit-for-tat attacks have intermittently flared.

The IRGC launched ballistic missiles toward a U.S. base in Jordan and hit U.S. oil tankers in September, after the U.S. military destroyed five Iranian oil tankers.

At the time, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) disputed Iran’s claim that it successfully struck the two American warships.

“No U.S. Navy warship has been struck; all IRGC attempted attacks failed,” Centcom wrote.

articles.title: Screwworm spreads to US wildlife in Texas, USDA says
articles.summary: The New World screwworm is a parasitic fly that can enter animals through open wounds and feed on living tissue.
articles.body:
( NewsNation ) — The first spread of the New World screwworm (NWS) in U.S. wildlife has been detected in Texas, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA).

The USDA’s Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service said Tuesday the screwworm was found in an elk.

According to the federal agency, the elk was reported after it was harvested by a hunter on a game ranch.

“This detection highlights the critical role hunters, landowners, outdoor enthusiasts, and wildlife professionals play in helping detect and stop the spread of NWS,” the USDA said in a news release.

Federal and state officials said they are expanding surveillance in the area and urging hunters, landowners and outdoor enthusiasts to watch for signs of infestation and report suspicious cases quickly to help prevent further spread.

First screwworm detection since FDA expanded treatments for the parasite

The USDA’s announcement follows the FDA’s June expansion of treatment options for animals aimed at fighting the flesh-eating parasite that poses a growing threat to livestock.

That same month, the USDA launched a 22,000-square-foot sterile fly production facility in Mexico that can produce up to 100 million flies to fight the parasite, which had been linked to 26 reported cases.

The New World screwworm is a parasitic fly that can enter animals through open wounds and feed on living tissue.

NewsNation’s Xavier Walton and Josie Fischels contributed to this report.

articles.title: Bill Gates says to prepare for 20 years of ‘tumultuous’ AI disruption
articles.summary: The Microsoft cofounder isn’t an AI doomer, but he says it’s still “the most dangerous weapon of all time.”
articles.body: Today, I’m talking to Bill Gates, cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft and chairman of the Gates Foundation. You may have noticed Bill in the news more lately — he’s been on something of a tour for the past few months, ever since publishing an essay in late August titled “The turbulent AI era is here. The choices we make now are critical.” In his piece, Gates ratcheted up his rhetoric around AI safety, writing that “even under the best circumstances, the transition to this new AI era will be one of the most turbulent times in human history.” In interviews since, Gates has called AI “the most dangerous thing that humans have ever gone near,” and that AI “makes nuclear weapons look like nothing.” It is clear he does not think the current policy response from the White House, or the lack of coordinated efforts from the AI industry itself, is sufficient to combat this threat. --- [Image: Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here. --- So I wanted to know: Is Bill Gates an AI doomer? I also had a series of questions downstream from what he’s been arguing about AI. How can we ever hope to control AI, and align it to humanity, if we can’t even agree on what it is and whether it’s conscious? How would you even technically construct a solution to alignment that could be enforced, not just for closed-source models but open-source ones, too? Bill gave us a big chunk of his time to dig into these issues with him, and the resulting conversation is a really illuminating one. He thinks we need to prepare for roughly two decades of AI disruption, and he says this period could be so painful it might split society in two — between people comfortable living near the technological frontier, and those who reject it. We also talked about the labor considerations, the nihilism of younger generations toward technological progress, and what should make us hopeful about the future. This is a deep one. Okay: Bill Gates, the cofounder and former CEO of Microsoft. Here we go. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Bill Gates, you are the co-founder and former CEO of Microsoft. You’re also the chairman of the Gates Foundation. Welcome to Decoder. Thank you. It’s good to talk to you again. You and I have spoken many times over the years. I would say that the circumstances of this conversation feel very different. Previously, when you and I would talk, you were always very hopeful about technology and what it could bring. You had a Netflix series a few years ago. You talked to The Verge, and I want to just read you this quote. You said, “I believe AI is a beneficial thing, we just need to shape it in the right way.” I would say you still agree with that, you just think the time to shape it is now. Yeah, I agree with that. I’d say the response broadly hasn’t been adequate to the speed that the challenge is arising. I’m very concerned that the bad stuff will not be minimized and that a lot of good stuff could come fairly slowly if we don’t manage it the right way. I want to have this conversation with you in three parts. I want to understand how you feel about AI as a technology today and why it’s advancing so quickly. I’m very curious about the technology, and the technical solutions to potentially control it. There are policy solutions as well, but it seems like we have to build an awful lot of technology. I’m also very curious to talk about who might impose those solutions and controls, because that seems very much up for debate right now as well. So let’s just start at the start. What has made you feel the urgency that AI is arriving at a speed that means we’re not ready to control it? The progress over the last year has been really quite amazing, starting with the ability to write code and find cyber flaws, the ability to reason in biology, the ability to form relationships with kids or other people, the ability to disrupt the job market. The incredible power that exists today means that every one of those things will happen and society needs to be ready. Do you see that happening as a technology as a whole or in the products that are instantiated by the companies that are making AI today? What I mean is that AI is a broad set of models that exist in the world, some open source, some proprietary. Then there are the companies that make these products and there are the leaders of those companies that make these products. At every level, there’s a different relationship you or I might have to AI. Are you seeing these risks and these capabilities broadly in the field, or in the particular companies led by the particular people? The risk isn’t one model versus another model. Certainly, the near-term danger of models where you can remove all the safeguards is very high and quite different from models where you monitor to make sure that cyberattackers and bioterrorists are not able to exploit the capability of the model to do gigantic harm. The big near-term risk really comes from models without safeguards. On a longer timeframe, the control issue relates to any state-of-the-art model, but it’s always easier when you can make sure safeguards are maintained. The reason I’m asking that question that way is maybe you don’t trust Sam Altman today, but you trust Dario Amodei.
